To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the speedups are superlinear in the size of the multiprocessor machine and that they are inherent, due both to the optimality and to the compatibility with the physical limitation.
parallelism and spatial locality combined may yield superlinear speedups and that this superlinearity can be achieved by multiprocessors whose interconnection network is a mesh of trees.
the speed of light is the limiting factor for multiprocessor machines and that the speedup of a machine is a function of its architecture and its memory hierarchy.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: (i) what is the maximum speedup that can be achieved by a multiprocessor with bounded-speed message propagation? and (ii) how should the multiprocessor be organized to achieve the maximum speedup?
the fundamental tradeoffs of the multiprocessor paradigm.
the fundamental question: How fast can a multiprocessor machine be?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the processor—time speedup tradeoffs of machines with hierarchical memory are very rich, complex, and interesting.
the processor—time product can be reduced by a factor of up to n log n by a suitable combination of locality and parallelism.
the processor—time performance of a parallel computer can be improved by using more processors, provided that they are used in a well-balanced manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the presence of bounded-speed propagation, the processor—time speedup of a multiprocessor machine is determined by the interplay of three factors: (i) the parallelism inherent in the algorithm, (ii) the locality of the algorithm, (iii) the locality of data.

the physical limitation expressed as bounded-speed propagation of message may be overcome by parallelism and locality, and that this may be accomplished by a careful orchestration of the simulation process.

the physical limitation of bounded-speed message propagation is a blessing rather than a curse for the design of parallel computers, and that the speedups achievable by multiprocessors with such a restriction can be arbitrarily close to the optimal ones.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, under bounded-speed message propagation, the speedup of parallel machines may be superlinear.
, for multiprocessors with bounded-speed message propagation, locality is more important than parallelism in achieving speedup.
the physical limitation on the speed of message propagation may be exploited to achieve superlinear speedups in a natural manner.
